1030.title: Awe walks
1030.hook: in a study, older adults who took weekly "awe walks" reported more joy (Sturm et al.)
1030.howItsDone: People who take awe walks go on ordinary walks with the intention of noticing vast and tiny things with fresh eyes; some walk the same route regularly, and some take a photo along the way.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Heschel. Your line was fearfully and wonderfully made. What ordinary thing got its second look? Last week belonged to scholars and naturalists. This week, the lab steps in. Day one thousand thirty.

Arm out, phone up, a quick selfie at the start of a walk. Same again halfway. Same again at the end. Week after week, a group of older adults did exactly this for a research team. The walks were short. Nobody climbed anything. And when the researchers later laid the photos side by side, something had shifted in the pictures of one group. The people in them took up less of the frame, and their smiles had changed. That group had been given one small extra instruction before they set out.
screen: `A SELFIE AT THE START.` → `WEEK AFTER WEEK.` → `SOMETHING SHIFTED IN THE FRAME.`

segments.voice: The study comes from Virginia Sturm and her colleagues. First, the setup. Everyone walked. One group just walked. The other was asked to take an awe walk: to go with fresh eyes, as if seeing things for the first time, and to notice what was vast and what was small. A cloud bank. A stretch of sky. The pattern on a leaf. Same legs, same shoes. The only change was where the attention went. Second, what the awe walkers reported. More awe, which you'd expect. But also more joy, and more of the warm, outward feelings, like gratitude and compassion. The researchers reported those gains growing over the weeks. Third, the photos. In the awe group, people took up less of their own selfies as time went on. More sky, more trees, more street; a little less self. Researchers call this the small self: the sense that you're one part of something larger. And the smiles in those photos grew stronger. Smaller, and happier, at the same time. Fourth, a walker from long before would have recognized this. Henry David Thoreau wrote an essay simply called Walking. He opens with the word saunter, and offers two playful stories of where it came from: wanderers heading to the Holy Land, or people with no particular home, at home everywhere. For Thoreau, even the shortest walk could be taken in a spirit of adventure. The study and the essayist land in the same place. You don't need a mountain. You need a different kind of looking, on the block you already know.
screen: `SAME WALK, DIFFERENT ATTENTION.` · `MORE JOY, MORE GRATITUDE.` · `A SMALLER SELF IN THE FRAME.` · `THOREAU'S SAUNTER.` · then, large: `SMALLER, AND HAPPIER.`

segments.voice: If you can stand and move, walk slowly: around the room, down a hallway, out a door. If you can't, look out the nearest window and let your eyes do the walking. Either way, give yourself the awe walk's one instruction: fresh eyes. Find one thing that is vast, a sky, a ceiling, a long view. Then one thing that is tiny, a crack, a thread, a leaf. Go back and forth between them. Let yourself be small for a minute. The bell holds the time.
Awe walks. Ordinary walks taken with fresh eyes, noticing the vast and the small. In one study, the walkers reported more joy. Today's word.

Your line: awe walk. Today, take one, even a short one, on a route you already know. Fresh eyes, the vast and the small. If you like, take a photo at the start and one at the end. Day one thousand thirty.

1031.title: Awe and time
1031.hook: a study found awe made people feel they had more time (Rudd, Vohs and Aaker)
1031.howItsDone: People who use awe this way pause in a rushed moment to look at something vast, such as the sky, the sea, or a wide view, and let their attention settle on the present before going back to the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the awe walk: fresh eyes, the vast and the small, and a smaller self in the photos. Your line was awe walk. Did you take one? Today, what awe might do to the clock. Day one thousand thirty-one.

How much time do you have right now? Not on the clock. In your body. Some days the answer is none at all. The inbox, the pickup, the dinner, the thing you promised. Minutes feel like coins falling through a hole in a pocket. Seneca, the Roman philosopher, wrote to a friend that time was the only thing truly ours, and that we let it slip away anyway. Centuries later, a team of researchers tried something odd. Instead of teaching people to manage time, they showed them something vast. Then they asked about the clock.
screen: `HOW MUCH TIME DO YOU HAVE?` → `COINS THROUGH A HOLE.` → `SHOW THEM SOMETHING VAST.`

segments.voice: The researchers were Melanie Rudd, Kathleen Vohs and Jennifer Aaker. First, the setup. They brought people into a feeling of awe, for example with a video of vast, astonishing scenes, or by having them recall or read about a moment of awe. Other people were brought into ordinary happiness, or into a neutral mood. Then everyone answered questions about time. Second, the finding in the title of their paper: awe expanded people's sense of time. The awe group reported feeling they had more time available, and feeling less impatient. Not more hours on the clock. A wider feeling of the hours they had. Third, what came with it. The awe group was more willing to give their time to help others, and leaned toward spending on experiences rather than things. Awe didn't just feel good; it seemed to loosen people's grip on their minutes. Fourth, why that might make sense. The researchers suggested that awe pulls a person into the present moment, and the present, fully noticed, seems to hold more. Seneca had already said what's at stake. In Richard Gummere's translation of his first letter: "Nothing, Lucilius, is ours, except time." The study adds a strange, hopeful twist. The way to more time may not be squeezing the day harder. It may be stopping, for a moment, in front of something bigger than the day.
screen: `AWE, HAPPINESS, OR NEUTRAL.` · `MORE TIME, LESS IMPATIENCE.` · `MORE WILLING TO GIVE TIME AWAY.` · `THE PRESENT HOLDS MORE.` · then, large: `NOTHING IS OURS, EXCEPT TIME.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind something vast: the ocean, a canyon, a night full of stars, or a view you've actually stood in front of. Stay with it. Don't check what time it is. Each time a task drifts in, notice it, and go back to the vast thing. Let the next breath be longer than the last. At the end, just notice: does the next hour look any different from here? The bell holds the time.
Melanie Rudd. Lead researcher of a study where people brought into awe reported feeling they had more time, and less impatience. Today's word.
Your line: more time. Today, at the moment you feel most rushed, stop for a few breaths and look at the biggest thing in view, even if it's only the sky. Day one thousand thirty-one.

what a scholar hears: Rudd, Vohs and Aaker's finding that awe expands perceived time, likely by pulling attention into the present.

1032.title: Awe and kindness
1032.hook: after gazing up at tall trees, people helped more in a study (Piff et al.)
1032.howItsDone: Some people make a habit of stopping under tall trees or in front of big views and looking up for a while, and then turning their attention to someone nearby who could use help.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Melanie Rudd's study on awe and the clock. Your line was more time. In your most rushed moment, did you find the biggest thing in view? Today, awe and the people around us. Day one thousand thirty-two.

A handful of pens hits the ground. The person who dropped them says oops and bends to gather them. You're standing right there. Do you crouch down and help, and how many do you pick up? It's a tiny moment, the kind nobody remembers by lunchtime. Which is exactly why a team of psychologists used it. They wanted to know whether something that happened just before, something that had nothing to do with pens, could change how many a stranger would pick up. What happened before was a minute of looking up.
screen: `A HANDFUL OF PENS.` → `DO YOU HELP?` → `A MINUTE OF LOOKING UP.`

segments.voice: The study was led by Paul Piff, with colleagues including Dacher Keltner. First, the setup. Some people stood in a grove of very tall eucalyptus trees and simply looked up into them for a short while. Others stood in the same spot but looked up at a tall building nearby. Same place, same task. Only the view was different. Second, the pens. Afterward, a researcher stumbled and dropped a handful of pens, apparently by accident. The people who had been gazing up at the trees picked up more of them. A small kindness, but measured. The tree group also reported feeling less entitled, less like the world owed them. Third, the explanation the researchers offered: the small self, the same idea that turned up in the awe walk selfies two days ago. Awe shrinks a person's sense of their own importance. Not in a crushing way, but in a way that makes room. In their account, under very tall trees a person's own concerns shrink back to size, and other people come back into view. Their other studies pointed the same direction: awe nudged people toward generosity. Fourth, trees and wonder have kept company for a long time. In the book of Psalms, in the King James words: "then shall all the trees of the wood rejoice." The poet pictures the trees themselves caught up in praise. The scientists never mentioned rejoicing trees. They counted pens. Two ways of standing among trees, and both begin by looking up. Tall trees, and a smaller self, and a hand reaching down to help.
screen: `TREES OR A BUILDING?` · `MORE PENS PICKED UP.` · `THE SMALL SELF MAKES ROOM.` · `THE TREES OF THE WOOD REJOICE.` · then, large: `TALL TREES, A SMALLER SELF.`

segments.voice: If there's a tall tree near you, go and stand under it, and look straight up into the branches. If not, find the tallest thing you can see from a window, or bring back the tallest tree you remember. Let your head tip back. Follow the trunk up, branch by branch, to where it meets the sky. Feel your own size against it. Then, before the bell, bring to mind one person nearby who could use a small hand today. The bell holds the time.
Paul Piff. The researcher whose study found that people who gazed up at tall trees helped a stranger more, in what he called the small self. Today's word.
Your line: tall trees. Today, look up at one tall tree, really look, and then do one small thing for someone nearby, the kind nobody will remember by lunchtime. Day one thousand thirty-two.

1033.title: Moral beauty
1033.hook: seeing great goodness gives a warm lift psychologists call elevation (Haidt)
1033.howItsDone: Some people deliberately seek out stories of great kindness, or recall the virtues of people they know, as a way to lift themselves and to prompt their own good deeds; Marcus Aurelius describes doing this in his Meditations.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul Piff's grove of eucalyptus and a handful of dropped pens. Your line was tall trees. Who got your small hand? Today, the awe that comes not from trees or stars, but from people. Day one thousand thirty-three.

Snow overnight. At six in the morning a teenager from down the street is already out with a shovel, clearing the driveway of the elderly woman next door. No one asked. No one is filming. He finishes, leans the shovel by her steps, and walks home. Some people who see a moment like that describe a warmth spreading in the chest, a lump in the throat, a sudden wish to go and do something good themselves. That reaction has a name, and a psychologist went looking for it.
screen: `SNOW, A SHOVEL, NO ONE ASKED.` → `A WARMTH IN THE CHEST.` → `A REACTION WITH A NAME.`

segments.voice: The psychologist is Jonathan Haidt, and the name he gave it is elevation. First, what it is. Elevation is the response to seeing someone act with unusual goodness: kindness, courage, generosity, forgiveness. Haidt calls that kind of goodness moral beauty. It's beauty, but in a deed instead of a sunset. Second, what it feels like, as people describe it. A warm or glowing feeling in the chest. Sometimes tears. A sense of being lifted, opened. Haidt set it beside disgust as its opposite: disgust is the feeling of watching people sink below the ordinary, and elevation is the feeling of watching someone rise above it. Third, what it does. In Haidt's research, people who felt elevation reported wanting to help others and to become better people themselves. Goodness, seen, seems to be catching. The feeling doesn't stay a feeling. In Haidt's account it points outward, toward other people, and toward the kind of person the watcher would like to be. Fourth, an old teacher who knew this. Marcus Aurelius, the Roman emperor who wrote private notes to himself, kept a habit of thinking about the good in the people around him. In George Long's translation: "When thou wishest to delight thyself, think of the virtues of those who live with thee." He didn't call it elevation. He used it as medicine. When he wanted delight, he went looking for someone's goodness on purpose. Moral beauty doesn't need a headline. It can turn up on an ordinary street, in small doses, for anyone watching for it.
screen: `MORAL BEAUTY: GOODNESS IN A DEED.` · `A WARMTH IN THE CHEST.` · `IT MAKES PEOPLE WANT TO HELP.` · `MARCUS LOOKS FOR VIRTUES.` · then, large: `THINK OF THE VIRTUES OF THOSE WHO LIVE WITH THEE.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind one great kindness you've seen, read about, or received. A stranger's, a parent's, a friend's, someone in the news. Go to the moment itself: the hands, the faces, what was said. Stay with it for a few breaths. Notice whether anything moves in your chest or your throat. Then, gently, notice whether it asks anything of you. You don't have to answer yet. If you pray, you can give thanks for that person in your own way. The bell holds the time.
Moral beauty. Unusual goodness, seen in a person's deed. Seeing it, some people describe a warm lift that Jonathan Haidt calls elevation. Today's word.
Your line: elevation. Today, watch or read about one great kindness on purpose, then tell someone about it, or pass a little of it on. Day one thousand thirty-three.

1034.title: Watch the sunrise
1034.howItsDone: People who make a practice of watching the sunrise get up before dawn, go somewhere with a view of the eastern sky, and watch quietly from first light until the sun is up; in several traditions, morning prayers gather around the hours of dawn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, moral beauty, and the warm lift of seeing goodness. Your line was elevation. Whose kindness did you pass on? The scientists have had their turn. Now we move to practices of awe, starting with a show that opens every morning. Day one thousand thirty-four.

Before the alarm, the window is the color of dishwater. Nothing has happened yet. Then the edge of the sky goes pale, then pink, then a color with no good name. Birds start before there's anything to see. The rooftops come out of the dark one by one. And then, at a single point on the horizon, a sliver of fire. Nobody pressed a button. Nobody earned it. It just arrives, the way it arrived yesterday and the day before, mostly while we were asleep.
screen: `THE COLOR OF DISHWATER.` → `PALE, PINK, NO GOOD NAME.` → `A SLIVER OF FIRE.`

segments.voice: Today the practice is the lesson: watch one sunrise, all the way through. First, why it works on people. A sunrise is vast and it is slow. You can't hurry it and you can't pause it. For once, the day comes to you, instead of you chasing the day. Second, in several traditions, the hours around dawn hold a special place in prayer. Muslims pray the dawn prayer, Fajr, before the sun comes up. Jews say the morning prayers of Shacharit as the day begins. Some Hindus offer water to the rising sun. Each tradition has its own reasons, and they aren't the same reasons. But each one gathers near the hours when the light changes. Third, a poet's picture. In the book of Psalms, the sun comes out "as a bridegroom coming out of his chamber, and rejoiceth as a strong man to run a race." A wedding and a race, at once. The psalm makes the sun sound eager, as if it's been waiting all night to begin. Fourth, Thoreau's warning. Near the very end of Walden he writes a line about dawn that isn't about the sky at all: "Only that day dawns to which we are awake." The sun comes up whether anyone is watching. But a day you sleep through, in body or in attention, never quite dawns for you. Watching a sunrise is a way of being awake for one, on purpose, start to finish. It arrives. The only question is whether anyone is there to meet it.
screen: `VAST, SLOW, AND UNEARNED.` · `PRAYERS AT THE CHANGING LIGHT.` · `A BRIDEGROOM, A RUNNER.` · `ONLY THAT DAY DAWNS TO WHICH WE ARE AWAKE.` · then, large: `IT ARRIVES.`

segments.voice: Turn toward the brightest window you have, or the brightest part of the room. If it's early and the sky is changing, watch it. If not, close your eyes and bring back a sunrise you've seen, or one you can imagine from where you sit. Follow it slowly: the dark, the pale edge, the colors, the first sliver. Don't rush to the end. Let the light come to you. Breathe as if you have all the time it takes. The bell holds the time.
Fajr. The Muslim dawn prayer, said before the sun comes up, one of several traditions' ways of greeting the whole arrival of a day. Today's word.
Your line: it arrives. Check when the sun comes up where you live, and set one alarm this week to watch it, start to finish, with no phone in your hand. Day one thousand thirty-four.

1035.title: The night sky
1035.hook: the stars you can see are only the nearest few
1035.howItsDone: People who practice stargazing as a practice of awe find a dark place away from lights, let their eyes adjust for several minutes, and look up without hurrying; some read Psalm 8, Job 38 or another text under the sky.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Fajr and the sunrise. Your line was it arrives. Did you set the alarm? Today we stay up for the other end of the day. Day one thousand thirty-five.

Step out of a lit kitchen into a dark yard and, at first, there's almost nothing up there. A few bright points. Maybe a plane. Give it a few minutes. Your eyes adjust, and more stars come out, then more, faint ones in between the bright ones, until the sky that looked empty looks crowded. Yet every one of those stars, even on the darkest, clearest night, is close by, as stars go. Neighbors. The ones you can see with your own eyes are only the nearest few.
screen: `OUT OF A LIT KITCHEN.` → `GIVE IT A FEW MINUTES.` → `ONLY THE NEAREST FEW.`

segments.voice: First, the size of what you're seeing. Astronomers say the stars visible to the naked eye all belong to our own galaxy, and to a small nearby part of it. Beyond them lie stars too faint to see, and beyond those, other galaxies. The night sky you can see is the front porch of something far larger. Second, the light. Starlight takes time to cross space, so each point is light that left its star long before tonight. You're looking at the past, all at once, from many different moments. Third, two old texts that looked up and heard different things. In the book of Job, the voice from the whirlwind turns the stars into questions Job can't answer. In the King James words: "Canst thou bind the sweet influences of Pleiades, or loose the bands of Orion?" The stars become a lesson in what Job cannot do. A psalm looks up at the same sky and asks a question of its own: "When I consider thy heavens, the work of thy fingers, the moon and the stars, which thou hast ordained; What is man, that thou art mindful of him?" And the psalm goes on to answer that this small creature is crowned with glory and honor. Humbled, and held. Both reactions are honest. Both start in the same place: someone standing still long enough to feel their size. Fourth, why it's a practice and not just a fact. You can read that the visible stars are only the nearest. It lands differently when you're standing in a dark yard, neck tipped back, and the sky keeps filling in the longer you stay.
screen: `THE NEAREST PART OF OUR GALAXY.` · `LIGHT THAT LEFT LONG AGO.` · `JOB'S STARS, THE PSALM'S QUESTION.` · `THE SKY FILLS IN AS YOU STAY.` · then, large: `WHAT IS MAN, THAT THOU ART MINDFUL OF HIM?`

segments.voice: If it's dark where you are, go to a window or a door, turn off the lights behind you, and look up. If it's daytime, close your eyes and bring back the darkest night sky you've ever seen. Either way, don't look for anything in particular. Let the sky fill in. Each breath, let one more faint star come out. Notice the distance. If you pray, you can let the psalm's question be part of your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Pleiades. One of the star clusters named in the book of Job, a reminder that every star you can see is a near neighbor, light from the past. Today's word.
Your line: the nearest stars. Tonight, go somewhere as dark as you can find and look up for five full minutes, long enough for your eyes to let the faint ones in. Day one thousand thirty-five.

1036.title: Watch the clouds
1036.howItsDone: Cloud watchers lie down or sit where they can see a wide stretch of sky and follow the clouds as they form and change, without hurrying and often without naming the shapes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the night sky and the Pleiades. Your line was the nearest stars. This week: awe walks, more time, tall trees, moral beauty, a sunrise, the stars. Science first, then practice. Today the week ends with an awe that's easy to find. Just look up. Day one thousand thirty-six.

A child lies on the grass and says, that one's a dragon. A minute later the dragon has lost its head and become a boat. A minute after that, the boat is coming apart into something with no name at all. Somewhere along the way, the game stops. Clouds turn into weather: will it rain, do I need a jacket. But the show never stopped. Right now, over every rooftop, shapes are forming that have never been seen before and won't be seen again. Clouds never repeat.
screen: `A DRAGON, THEN A BOAT.` → `CLOUDS BECOME WEATHER.` → `SHAPES THAT NEVER RETURN.`

segments.voice: First, what a cloud is. Not a thing, really. An event. Water rises as vapor, cools, and gathers into countless tiny drops on specks of dust, and the cloud is the shape that water takes for a while before it changes again. It's always being made and unmade at once. That's why no two are ever the same. Second, an old line that watched the same cycle. Ecclesiastes, in the King James words: "All the rivers run into the sea; yet the sea is not full; unto the place from whence the rivers come, thither they return again." The writer saw water going round and round, and a cloud is that water on its way back up. Third, a philosopher who built a whole teaching on change. Heraclitus, the ancient Greek thinker, is remembered, through later writers, for saying you can't step into the same river twice. A later summary of his teaching boiled it down to two Greek words: panta rhei, everything flows. Fourth, why watching clouds is a practice of awe. It's free. It needs no travel and no alarm. And it trains the eye on something that won't hold still for you. The cloud you're looking at is never the same as it was a breath ago. Neither, if you look closely, is the one looking.

segments.voice: Find a window with some sky in it, or step outside. If there are clouds, pick one. If the sky is clear, pick a patch of blue and wait for whatever drifts through. Watch one edge of the cloud. Don't name the shape; just watch it change. When it becomes something else, let it. When it thins, let it. Breathe slowly, and let your attention move as slowly as the cloud does. The bell holds the time.
Panta rhei. Heraclitus's two Greek words for everything flows, the teaching behind watching clouds that form, change and never return. Today's word.
Your line: never the same. Today, give the clouds three full minutes, lying on grass if you can, at a window if you can't. Let one dragon become a boat. Day one thousand thirty-six.
